headings.title: Introduction and Purpose of Foetal Circulation
headings.content: Inside the womb, a foetus cannot breathe air or eat solid food. The developing baby relies entirely on the mother's placenta for oxygen and nutrients while getting rid of metabolic waste. Foetal circulation is specially designed to bypass the non-functioning lungs and liver, routing oxygen-rich blood directly to vital organs like the brain and heart. Unlike adult circulation where the right and left sides of the heart are completely separate, the foetal circulatory system uses special vascular structures called shunts to redirect blood flow. Understanding this unique setup is vital for nurses caring for pregnant mothers and newborns in Nigerian hospitals, as it explains how the baby survives prenatal life and how the body suddenly rewires itself during delivery.

headings.title: Key Anatomical Structures and Shunts
headings.content:
The foetal circulatory system relies on three unique vascular structures that close shortly after birth. Nurses must be familiar with these pathways to understand congenital heart defects and neonatal transition:
- **Ductus Venosus**: A shunt that allows oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to bypass the liver sinusoidal network and empty directly into the inferior vena cava.
- **Foramen Ovale**: An opening between the right and left atria that shunts blood away from the pulmonary circulation directly into the systemic circulation.
- **Ductus Arteriosus**: A blood vessel connecting the main pulmonary artery to the descending aorta, diverting blood away from the fluid-filled lungs.

headings.title: Pathway of Oxygenated Blood from the Placenta
headings.content: Oxygen and nutrient-rich blood leaves the placenta through a single umbilical vein. As this blood approaches the foetal abdomen, a portion goes to the liver, but the majority travels through the ductus venosus to merge with the inferior vena cava. Here, it mixes with a smaller amount of deoxygenated blood returning from the lower body. This mixed blood enters the right atrium. Because of the anatomical angle of the Eustachian valve, most of this well-oxygenated blood shoots straight through the foramen ovale into the left atrium. From the left atrium, it moves to the left ventricle and out the aorta, ensuring the brain and upper extremities receive the highest possible oxygen concentration.

headings.title: Deoxygenated Blood Journey and Return to Placenta
headings.content: Deoxygenated and nutrient-depleted blood from the upper body returns via the superior vena cava into the right atrium. Unlike the oxygenated stream crossing the foramen ovale, this blood passes down into the right ventricle and into the pulmonary trunk. Since the pulmonary vascular resistance is very high in utero, only a small fraction enters the lungs. The bulk of this blood passes through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta, supplying the lower body and viscera. Ultimately, two umbilical arteries—branches of the internal iliac arteries—carry this spent blood away from the foetus back to the placenta for waste elimination and re-oxygenation.

headings.title: Transition from Foetal to Neonatal Circulation
headings.content: At birth, the cutting of the umbilical cord and the baby's first breath trigger massive hemodynamic changes. Air enters the lungs, causing pulmonary vascular resistance to drop sharply while pulmonary blood flow increases. This rise in left atrial pressure physically pushes the flap of the foramen ovale closed. Simultaneously, increased blood oxygen levels and a drop in prostaglandins cause the ductus arteriosus to constrict and eventually fibrose. The ductus venosus also collapses as blood flow from the umbilical cord ceases. These functional closures turn the temporary shunts into permanent fibrous remnants within the first few weeks of life.

headings.title: Common Clinical Implications and Congenital Anomalies
headings.content: Sometimes, the complex closing process of foetal structures fails, leading to congenital heart conditions. A persistent connection between the aorta and pulmonary artery is known as a patent ductus arteriosus, which causes extra blood to flood the lungs and stresses the heart. If the foramen ovale fails to seal, it becomes an atrial septal defect, allowing abnormal blood mixing. Premature babies in neonatal units are especially prone to a patent ductus arteriosus because their blood vessels are less responsive to oxygen changes. Midwives and nurses must monitor neonatal vital signs, respiratory effort, and heart murmurs closely during the transition period to catch these anomalies early.
